title: Why are we making these mistakes again?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou argues that England's government is unpicking one of the few public policy successes of recent decades by reviving four reforms from the mid-2000s: incentivised vocational qualifications for 14 to 16 year olds, speaking and listening assessment, removal of the EBacc, and generic skills statements. Drawing on her own training year in 2007, she shows how each of these went wrong the first time, from vocational awards with little labour market value to oracy coursework that inflated grades and foreign language numbers that collapsed once the incentive went. She then tests the government's rationale that the Conservative reforms caused rising NEET rates and falling enjoyment of reading, and finds that Wales and Scotland, which took different paths, show the same or worse trends. Her central point is that curriculum reform trades in a scarce resource, time, so protecting English and maths does not protect academic standards when other subjects are squeezed. She also notes that the same pressure falls on senior leaders' attention. The piece is a policy polemic, but its evidence rests on a clear comparative check across the UK nations.
points: Christodoulou frames the four policies as a rerun of 2007-era reforms, so they can be judged on how they performed the first time rather than on rhetoric about their promise.

A simple UK nations check undermines the claim that England's reforms caused NEET growth or a decline in reading enjoyment, because Wales and Scotland show similar or worse trends under different policies.
Literacy and numeracy are among the best attested drivers of labour market success, which makes the argument that academic standards harm employability implausible.
Time is the scarce currency of curriculum reform, so incentivising new vocational qualifications squeezes history, languages and design and technology even when English and maths are ring-fenced.
She warns that generic skills grids are returning without institutional memory of why earlier versions proved unreliable and time-consuming.
quotes: Essentially, even with all the structural reasons that have made it harder for teens to get jobs, it is likely that one of the best ways to avoid NEETdom is to do well at maths and English.
There is an entire research literature on how literacy and numeracy lead to better performance in the job market. It is one of the best attested findings in education economics.
If Conservative education reforms were causing NEET rates to spike, we’d expect to see the increase in England only, or at least a bigger and faster increase in England. But we don’t.

Again, it is true that the proportion of children in the UK reporting that they enjoy reading has fallen dramatically, from 54% in 2014 to just 36% in 2026. However, all these numbers and trends are very similar across England (55% to 36%), Wales (53% to 33%) and Scotland (55% to 37%).
It took a lot of teacher and class time to administer, was very hard to grade reliably, and ended up being a contributor to grade inflation.
There seems to be very little institutional memory within the DfE of all the problems these types of statements cause.

This is because curriculum and assessment reforms are dealing with a fundamentally scarce resource: time. People often think money is the biggest constraint, and it is certainly a constraint, but budgets can be increased in a way that time cannot.

If you look at the most high-functioning organisations in the public and private sector, they tend to be organised around a couple of important priorities. You can’t prioritise everything. If one thing is a top priority, then by definition something else is not.
